name: enumerateDevices label gating
plain: Lists camera, microphone and speaker counts; names only after permission.
meaning: Reveals how many cameras, mics and speakers exist (before consent, labels empty), and device names after consent. Counts and kinds are a mild fingerprint and show setup type.

access.prompt_ui: No prompt for the counts; labels appear once the origin has an active camera or microphone grant.
access.iframe: Not delegated; follows the frame's own grants
steps: Receive list with kind and deviceId
Labels empty until getUserMedia has been granted
Listen to devicechange for plug events

data.metric: Devices with kind, deviceId, groupId and label

fields.name: groupId
fields.range: shared by a physical device's inputs and outputs

limits.headline: Can count your cameras, mics and speakers, but names stay hidden until you allow access
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a call or recording page loads
can: Tell how many cameras, microphones and speakers you have
Find out which kinds of devices exist before asking for access
Show device names after you have allowed the camera or microphone
cannot: See device names before the site has camera or microphone access
Turn any device on or capture anything by itself
Show a prompt, so you only know it happened if the site tells you

story.what_it_is: Lets a site count your cameras, mics and speakers, and see their names only after you allow access.

marketing.name: enumerateDevices
marketing.pitch: Developer docs say it lists media input and output devices, with labels hidden until the person grants access.

story.for_you: You never see this one run. It happens in the background as a call page loads, so the site can show you a camera picker. Before you allow access, it only learns how many devices you have, not their names.
story.for_makers: Call sites need a list of devices to build the camera and mic picker, and to pick a sensible default. Fraud and ad scripts can also use the device counts as one small clue in a device fingerprint. The maker gets setup data without asking you a thing.

use_cases.example: A web call opens a settings panel with a drop down of your headset, built in laptop mic and webcam, so you can choose the right one.
A browser game with voice chat lists your microphones, so you can pick your headset and not the laptop mic.
A fraud check notices a visitor has no cameras or mics at all, which is common for bots in a cloud server, and adds a risk point.
An ad script quietly counts your audio and video devices, and combines them with your screen size and fonts to build a device ID.
A streaming page checks whether a webcam is present before showing a Go live button, so it does not offer the feature when it cannot work.
A support tool logs device counts when a call fails, so engineers can see that a customer with no mic was stuck.

risks: Counts add to a device fingerprint

technical_bounds: Device ids reset when site data is cleared
No serial numbers or vendor ids

abuse: Counting devices to tell setup type

linkedin.how: LinkedIn script enumerates devices and records kinds and counts without labels

history.change: Safari returns no devices when permission is denied and stops checking permission in enumerateDevices
